name: Kneeling or balance-ball chair

lead: Kneeling chairs and balance-ball chairs open the angle at the hips so the spine sits more upright and the lower-back curve is kept, instead of a slouched sit. The aim is a taller, straighter seated posture.

A sloped seat with shin rests tilts the pelvis forward, and a ball seat asks the body to make small balance adjustments. Small studies have measured lumbar curve, hip loading and muscle activity; they did not measure how people look.

paras: People use them for part of the workday, often alternating with a regular chair, since kneeling chairs are usually used intermittently. They are paired with standing breaks and posture exercises.
Studies report discomfort measures but no documented serious harms. Kneeling chairs load the shins and knees, and some users find long sessions tiring.

angle.text: Kneeling and balance-ball chairs open the hip angle so the spine sits more upright while you are seated on them. Small studies have measured lumbar curve and muscle activity.

lead: A kneeling chair supports the user with a forward-sloping seat and padded shin rests, so the thighs sit about 60 to 70 degrees from vertical rather than the usual 90 and part of the body weight rests on the shins. [1][2] A balance-ball chair uses an inflated exercise ball, or a ball held in a frame, as the seat. [3] Both are sold as forms of active seating that encourage an upright torso during desk work.

People use them for appearance through posture. The proposed chain runs from a more open hip angle, to a pelvis that tilts forward and keeps the lower back's natural curve, to a taller, less slumped sitting posture and fewer hours spent rounded forward over a keyboard. Proponents also say the chairs wake the core muscles, the same reasoning behind sitting on an exercise ball. [1][3]

The modern kneeling chair is credited to Norwegian designer Hans Christian Mengshoel's Balans chair, with later designs by Peter Opsvik, Oddvin Rykken and Svein Gusrud. [1][2][4] Published studies have measured lumbar curvature, hip loading and muscle activity in kneeling configurations, mostly in small samples. [5][6][7][8][9] Those studies measure spinal shape and muscle activity; none has measured how a person looks.
infobox: Peter Opsvik, Oddvin Rykken, Svein Gusrud [2][4]
Rocker-base kneeling chair, wheeled office kneeling chair, saddle chair, stability-ball chair [1][2][3]
Swiss ball, molded by Aquilino Cosani in 1963 [3]
Intermittent sessions alongside a standard chair or standing desk [1]

paras: A kneeling chair has a forward-tilted seat, often about 20 degrees from horizontal, and shin rests positioned in front of it. Most of the weight stays on the buttocks while the shin rests stop the sitter from sliding forward [1][2]. Many models have a curved rocker base that allows slight forward and backward movement; office versions use a gas lift for height and may add casters [1].

A balance-ball chair replaces the seat with an exercise ball, sometimes within a wheeled frame that adds a back support. The ball itself was developed as the Swiss ball in 1963 by Italian plastics manufacturer Aquilino Cosani, and came into therapy use through physiotherapists in Switzerland and later the United States [3].

Wikipedia credits Hans Christian Mengshoel with the original modern kneeling chair, the Balans chair, in 1979, noting that the date needs a citation; Grokipedia places Mengshoel's concept in 1976, describes inspiration from traditional seiza sitting and says prototypes were shown at the 1979 Scandinavian Furniture Fair in Copenhagen. [2][1] Norwegian designers Oddvin Rykken, Peter Opsvik and Svein Gusrud later developed chairs on the same principle. [2]

Opsvik (1939 to 2024) is also known for the Tripp Trapp children's chair (1972), the Capisco saddle chair and the 2009 book Rethinking Sitting, which set out an approach to dynamic sitting in which people change position rather than hold one. [4] Kneeling chairs were among the first furniture designed for use with computers and were sold as computer chairs. [2] Grokipedia says Norwegian firms such as Varier and Håg mass-produced them in the 1980s, that adoption grew in the 1990s with concern over repetitive strain injuries, and that interest rose again with remote work after 2020. [1]

Research interest followed. A 1985 study by Drury and Francher on the Balans chair concluded it was no better than conventional chairs, whereas a 1989 study of 20 subjects reported greater lumbar curvature on a kneeling chair than on a straight-back chair, and a 1987 study reported effects on blood circulation, according to Wikipedia. [2] Ergonomist A. C. Mandal's work from the 1960s to the 1990s supported forward-sloping seats for opening the torso-thigh angle. [2]

The exercise ball began as the Swiss ball, developed in 1963 by Italian plastics manufacturer Aquilino Cosani using a molding process for large, puncture-resistant balls. Swiss pediatrician Elsbeth Köngan is credited with probably starting its therapy use, British physiotherapist Mary Quinton used Pezzi balls with infants in Switzerland, and Susanne Klein-Vogelbach built ball exercise into neuro-developmental physical therapy, with a 1985 book. [3]

Joanne Posner-Mayer's 1995 book brought the ball approach to orthopedic and sports medicine in the United States. Balls come in five diameters from 35 to 95 cm and are used in training, yoga and Pilates; sitting on one as an office chair followed from this use. [3]

In a conventional chair the torso-thigh angle is about 90 degrees, which tends to roll the pelvis backward and flatten the lumbar curve. A kneeling chair opens that angle toward 110 degrees or more, which proponents say lets the pelvis stay neutral and the spine stack upright without a backrest. [1] A model of a virtual male population estimated lower hip flexion and lower hip joint reaction force in a kneeling configuration than in a simple chair or car seat. [5] Grokipedia reports hip flexion of about 51 degrees and a hip force of 59 N versus 124 N on a simple chair. [1]

Proponents add that the lack of a backrest means the core muscles work to hold the trunk, and that the open hip angle promotes easier breathing. [1] A ball seat is unstable, so trunk muscles work to keep balance, a principle called unstable training. Wikipedia notes that studies showed more abdominal activity in exercises done on an unstable surface, but states that there is no scientific evidence of benefits from simply sitting on the ball without additional exercises. [3]

Findings on lumbar curve are positive but small. A 2008 comparison found that an ergonomic kneeling chair at a +20 degree inclination maintained lumbar curvature closer to standing than a standard computer chair. [6] Grokipedia reports a mean difference of 7.6 degrees from standing at that setting. [1] A pilot study of 10 patients with chronic low back pain and 10 matched controls measured pelvic and lumbar parameters on radiographs in different chairs and postures [7], and a radiographic study of 20 asymptomatic subjects compared standing with several seated variants. [8] A 2026 study tested four seat-angle and knee-rest combinations for muscle activity and perceived discomfort. [9]

Results across decades point in different directions: the 1985 Drury and Francher comparison found no advantage over conventional chairs, a 1989 study reported greater lumbar curvature on the Balans chair, and Grokipedia notes a 1989 report of greater spinal compression on the Balans chair than on a standard chair. [2][1] Grokipedia describes long-term evidence for back-pain relief as inconclusive. [1]

Wikipedia's article on sitting says recent research finds no clear causal link between posture and back pain and that workplace chair changes showed moderate evidence for reducing musculoskeletal symptoms, while therapy ball chairs are listed among interventions with mixed results. [10]

Wikipedia notes that a common belief is that kneeling chairs load the knees, while most weight actually remains on the buttocks. [2] Grokipedia lists added pressure on the knees and shins, with a 1985 study reporting discomfort after about 2.5 hours, and notes that the position may be unsuitable for people with knee problems or arthritis; typical weight limits are 250 to 300 lb. [1]

Because there is no backrest, discomfort over long periods is a common report; one T Nation poster describes hips and knees feeling 'terrible' after sitting too long in a kneeling office chair. [11] Grokipedia says these chairs are typically used intermittently, often starting with 15 to 30 minute sessions and alternating with standard chairs or standing desks. [1] Wikipedia notes that people using a ball as an office seat can find it uncomfortable because of the lack of back support. [3]

Kneeling and ball chairs come up in posture and desk-ergonomics discussion as part of correcting slumped sitting, usually alongside exercises for the back and neck. In community material they are mentioned mainly in passing and in training logs; the appearance goals people name are a taller seated posture, less rounded upper back and forward head, and a stronger core. [11]

Features described for kneeling chairs include adjustable seat and shin-rest height (Grokipedia gives a range of roughly 21 to 31 inches), adjustable shin-rest angle, rocker or caster bases, padding thickness, optional armrests or a low backrest, and materials such as beech wood, molded plastic and metal. [1] Grokipedia cites a global market of about 200 million US dollars in 2024, adding that its sources include retailer pages. [1]
Ball chairs differ in ball size, anti-burst rating and whether a frame adds back support. [3]

A modelling study of a virtual male population estimated hip joint reaction force and hip flexion angle for a simple chair, a car seat and a kneeling chair, and reported a lower force in the kneeling configuration [5]. A study asked whether ergonomic kneeling chairs preserve lumbar curvature better than a standard computer chair and found they did at +20 degrees of inclination [6]. A pilot study of 10 patients with chronic low back pain and 10 matched controls measured pelvic and lumbar parameters on radiographs [7]. A radiographic study of 20 asymptomatic subjects compared standing with several seated variants [8]. A 2026 study assessed four kneeling chair angle combinations for muscle activity and perceived discomfort [9]. No studies of balance-ball chairs were found among the research reviewed here, and none of the studies tests either chair for appearance.

lore.intro: Kneeling and ball chairs come up in lifting and ergonomics forums as seating experiments, with mixed personal reports.

claims.claim: A kneeling chair keeps the spine upright and reduces slouching.
Sitting on a ball builds core strength.
A kneeling chair can become uncomfortable after long periods.
Posture seating fixes slouching and back problems.
